summary: For learners aged 11-13, the goal is to move from recognising triangles, quadrilaterals and circles to DERIVING and justifying their properties (interior angles, diagonals, symmetry, side relationships) and reasoning about how shapes relate hierarchically. The signature idea is class-inclusion classification: a square is a special case of BOTH a rectangle and a rhombus because it has all their defining properties and more. The documented core obstacle is prototype/partition thinking — pupils who can state definitions still judge by the prototypical picture, denying 'a square is a rectangle', and often miss the opposing-direction and transitive inclusions (square ⊆ rhombus ⊆ parallelogram ⇒ square ⊆ parallelogram). For circles, properties are relational: diameter = 2 × radius and circumference = π × diameter, with π a constant ratio independent of the circle's size. Effective teaching derives properties by construction and measurement, builds from hierarchical (not partition) definitions, and uses dynamic (or adjustable) shapes so a learner can watch one shape become a special case of another without losing the general properties, with hands-on construction, measurement and comparison supporting the same ideas.
misconceptions: Partition/prototype classification: denying that a square is a rectangle (or a rhombus) because the shapes 'look different' or a rectangle 'must have two long and two short sides'
One-directional / non-transitive inclusion: accepting square ⊆ rhombus but not square ⊆ parallelogram, or thinking a rectangle cannot share square properties
Judging properties by appearance rather than derivation — e.g. assuming a parallelogram's diagonals are equal (confusing it with a rectangle)
Confusing radius and diameter, or believing π (circumference ÷ diameter) depends on the size of the circle
Treating each named shape as an isolated category with no overlapping membership

activities.title: Morph a rectangle into a square and watch inclusion persist
steps: Start with a 'long' rectangle and list which names currently fit it: note that, of the names parallelogram, rectangle, rhombus and square, only 'rectangle' and 'parallelogram' apply (it is also a quadrilateral).
Change the shape by moving its corners/sides until all four sides are equal, keeping the four right angles.
Observe that 'rhombus' and 'square' now apply too — while 'rectangle' never stopped applying.
Say in your own words why the square never stopped being a rectangle: it kept every rectangle property and simply gained the extra property of four equal sides.
activities.insight: A square is a special case of a rectangle (and of a rhombus): it satisfies every defining property of the more general class and adds more, so it belongs to both classes at once.

activities.title: Derive diagonal and symmetry properties by folding and measuring
steps: Construct or cut out a parallelogram, a rectangle and a rhombus (paper/card approximations of the ideal flat figures).

Draw the diagonals; fold and measure to test: do the diagonals bisect each other? Are they equal in length? Do they meet at right angles? Also fold along each diagonal and along each line joining midpoints of opposite sides to test which are lines of symmetry.

Record for each shape which diagonal and symmetry properties hold, e.g. a parallelogram's diagonals bisect each other but are NOT generally equal, whereas a rectangle's diagonals ARE equal and a rhombus's diagonals meet at right angles; a non-square rectangle's lines of symmetry join midpoints of opposite sides (its diagonals are NOT lines of symmetry), a non-square rhombus's lines of symmetry are its diagonals, and a parallelogram that is neither has no line of symmetry.
State each property as something you checked by construction/measurement, not something you guessed from the picture.
activities.insight: Properties should be derived and verified, not read off appearance; different classes have genuinely different diagonal/symmetry properties, which is how you can tell them apart and justify inclusion.

activities.title: Measure several circles to let π emerge as a constant ratio
steps: Collect several circular objects of different sizes (tins, lids) and some string or tape.
Before measuring, PREDICT how many times the diameter will fit around the circumference, and say WHY — in particular, predict whether the answer changes with the size of the circle.
Wrap and measure the circumference, then measure the diameter, for each object.
Compute circumference ÷ diameter for each and compare: the ratio should come out a little more than 3 (close to 3.14, within measuring error) each time, regardless of the circle's size.
Also check that the diameter is twice the radius (d = 2r) and state circumference = π × diameter in your own words.
activities.insight: Radius, diameter and circumference are related multiplicatively: d = 2r and C = πd, where π is a constant ratio (≈ 3.14) that does NOT depend on the size of the circle.

activities.title: Always / sometimes / never and the inclusion chain
steps: Decide for each statement whether it is always, sometimes or never true, and justify by properties: 'A square is a rectangle', 'A rectangle is a square', 'A square is a rhombus', 'A square is a parallelogram'.
Trace the inclusion chain square ⊆ rhombus ⊆ parallelogram and explain why it follows that a square is a parallelogram (transitive reasoning).
Explain why 'a square is a rectangle' is always true but 'a rectangle is a square' is only sometimes true — the two directions are different.
Build or complete a family-tree / Venn diagram of parallelogram, rectangle, rhombus and square, placing each shape in every class it belongs to.
activities.insight: Inclusion has a direction and is transitive: the more special shape belongs to the more general classes, but not the reverse; chaining inclusions lets you conclude square ⊆ parallelogram.

activities.title: 'Convince me a square is a rectangle' — a reasoning dialogue
steps: Take the position that a square IS a rectangle and argue it to a partner or teacher who keeps pushing back with prototype objections ('but rectangles are long', 'they look different').
For each objection, answer by checking the square against a specific defining property of a rectangle (four right angles, opposite sides equal and parallel).
Conclude with a property-based statement: a square has every rectangle property and adds four equal sides, so it is a special rectangle.
activities.insight: A convincing justification of inclusion is built from checking defining properties, and it withstands appearance-based objections.

checkQuestion: Answer each with yes or no, then explain: Is a square a rectangle? Is a square a rhombus? Use the properties of these shapes in your reasoning.
checkAnswer: Yes to both. A square IS a rectangle because it has every defining property of a rectangle — four right angles and opposite sides equal and parallel — and simply adds the extra property that all four sides are equal, so it is a special rectangle. A square IS a rhombus because it has the rhombus's defining property of four equal sides, adding right angles, so it is a special rhombus. The reasoning must be property-based inclusion (the square satisfies all the properties of the more general class), not 'they look different'.
